q01.question: How much time does a company have to answer a person who asks to see or delete their data?
q01.answer: A controller must provide information on action taken regarding a data subject request (such as for access or deletion) without undue delay and in any event within one month of receiving the request `[gdpr, Article 12(3)]`. This period may be extended by two further months where necessary, taking into account the complexity and number of requests, provided the controller informs the data subject of the extension and reasons for the delay within one month of receipt `[gdpr, Article 12(3)]`.

q03.question: If a person is harmed because a company broke the data protection rules, who can they claim compensation from?
q03.answer: A person who has suffered material or non-material damage from an infringement can claim compensation from the controller or processor involved in the processing [gdpr, Article 82(1)]. While any controller involved is liable for damage caused by infringing processing, a processor is liable only if it failed to comply with GDPR obligations specifically directed to processors or acted outside or contrary to lawful instructions of the controller [gdpr, Article 82(2)]. Where multiple controllers or processors are responsible, each can be held liable for the entire damage to ensure effective compensation [gdpr, Article 82(4)].

q02.question: In which situations must a company appoint a data protection officer?
q02.answer:
A controller or processor must designate a data protection officer (DPO) if:
*   The processing is carried out by a public authority or body (except for courts acting in their judicial capacity) [gdpr, Article 37(1)(a)];
*   The core activities of the controller or processor consist of processing operations that require regular and systematic monitoring of data subjects on a large scale [gdpr, Article 37(1)(b)]; or
*   The core activities consist of processing on a large scale of special categories of data or personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences [gdpr, Article 37(1)(c)].

Additionally, a DPO must be designated where required by Union or Member State law [gdpr, Article 37(4)].

q04.question: A company loses a USB stick with unencrypted customer data and cannot tell whether anyone read it. Does it still have to report the breach?
q04.answer: Yes, the loss of a USB stick with unencrypted personal data must be notified [edpb_breach_notification, para 33 (p.11)]. Even if it is impossible to ascertain whether unauthorized persons accessed the data, the loss constitutes an availability breach, and the controller becomes "aware" of the breach when they realize the USB stick is missing [edpb_breach_notification, para 33 (p.11)].

q05.question: Can a company send one single report to the authority for several similar data breaches?
q05.answer: Yes, a controller may submit a "bundled" notification for several similar breaches to avoid being overly burdensome [edpb_breach_notification, para 64 (p.16)]. This is permissible provided the breaches concern the same type of personal data, were breached in the same way, and occurred over a relatively short period of time [edpb_breach_notification, para 64 (p.16)]. If the breaches involve different types of data or were caused in different ways, they should generally be reported individually in accordance with Article 33 [edpb_breach_notification, para 64 (p.16)].

q06.answer: A processor (such as an IT provider) must notify the controller of a personal data breach without undue delay [gdpr, Article 33(2); edpb_breach_notification, para 44 (p.13)]. q10.question: If hackers steal encrypted customer data, does the company still have to report the breach, and does it have to tell the customers?
q10.answer:
Whether a company must report a breach of encrypted data depends on whether the breach poses a risk to individuals' rights and freedoms [edpb_breach_notification, para 78 (p.19)]. *   The encryption key is compromised or the encryption software is vulnerable [edpb_breach_notification, para 78 (p.19), para 79 (p.19)].
*   There are no adequate backups, leading to an availability breach that poses risks to individuals [edpb_breach_notification, para 76 (p.18), para 79 (p.19)].
*   The loss of data, even if encrypted, results in a lack of availability that negatively affects individuals [edpb_breach_notification, para 79 (p.19)].

If the breach is unlikely to result in a risk to individuals, notification to the supervisory authority and the data subjects is generally not required, though the risk must be re-evaluated if circumstances change [edpb_breach_notification, para 78 (p.19)].

q14.question: When are two companies considered to be deciding jointly about the same data, and what must they arrange between themselves if they are?
q14.answer:
Two companies are considered joint controllers when they jointly determine the purposes and means of a specific processing activity, meaning they have a decisive influence over whether and how the processing takes place [gdpr, Article 26(1); edpb_controller_processor, para 51 (p.19), para 54 (p.19)]. This joint participation can result from a common decision or converging decisions that are necessary for the processing to occur [edpb_controller_processor, front matter (p.1), para 54 (p.19)].

If they are joint controllers, they must determine their respective responsibilities for compliance with the GDPR—particularly regarding data subject rights and information duties—by means of a transparent arrangement [gdpr, Article 26(1)]. This arrangement should reflect their actual roles and relationships, and its essence must be made available to the data subject [gdpr, Article 26(2)]. The EDPB recommends that this arrangement be a binding document, such as a contract, to ensure legal certainty, transparency, and accountability [edpb_controller_processor, front matter (p.1)]. Regardless of this arrangement, data subjects may exercise their rights against each of the controllers [gdpr, Article 26(3)].

q15.answer:
The controller is responsible for carrying out a data protection impact assessment (DPIA) prior to processing when a type of processing is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons [gdpr, Article 35(1)].

A DPIA is specifically required for:
*   Systematic and extensive evaluation of personal aspects based on automated processing (including profiling) that produces legal or similarly significant effects [gdpr, Article 35(3)(a)].
*   Processing on a large scale of special categories of data or personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences [gdpr, Article 35(3)(b)].
*   Systematic monitoring of a publicly accessible area on a large scale [gdpr, Article 35(3)(c)].

When carrying out the assessment, the controller must seek the advice of their data protection officer, if one has been designated [gdpr, Article 35(2)].

q26.question: What does a data protection authority have to take into account when deciding how big a fine should be?
q26.answer:
When deciding on the amount of an administrative fine, a supervisory authority must ensure the fine is effective, proportionate, and dissuasive in each individual case [gdpr, Article 83(1)].

The authority must give due regard to the following factors:
*   The nature, gravity, and duration of the infringement, including the nature, scope, or purpose of the processing, the number of data subjects affected, and the level of damage suffered [gdpr, Article 83(2)(a)].
*   Whether the infringement was intentional or negligent [gdpr, Article 83(2)(b)].
*   Actions taken to mitigate the damage [gdpr, Article 83(2)(c)].
*   The degree of responsibility, considering technical and organisational measures implemented [gdpr, Article 83(2)(d)].
*   Any relevant previous infringements [gdpr, Article 83(2)(e)].
*   The degree of cooperation with the supervisory authority [gdpr, Article 83(2)(f)].
*   The categories of personal data affected [gdpr, Article 83(2)(g)].
*   The manner in which the infringement became known to the authority, including whether it was notified [gdpr, Article 83(2)(h)].
*   Compliance with previously ordered measures [gdpr, Article 83(2)(i)].
*   Adherence to approved codes of conduct or certification mechanisms [gdpr, Article 83(2)(j)].
*   Any other aggravating or mitigating factors, such as financial benefits gained or losses avoided [gdpr, Article 83(2)(k)].

q27.question: What are the three kinds of personal data breach?
q27.answer:
Personal data breaches can be categorized into the following three types based on information security principles [edpb_breach_notification, para 17 (p.7)]:

*   **Confidentiality breach:** Unauthorized or accidental disclosure of, or access to, personal data [edpb_breach_notification, para 17 (p.7)].
*   **Integrity breach:** Unauthorized or accidental alteration of personal data [edpb_breach_notification, para 17 (p.7)].
*   **Availability breach:** Accidental or unauthorized loss of access to, or destruction of, personal data [edpb_breach_notification, para 17 (p.7)].

A breach may involve one, two, or all three of these categories simultaneously [edpb_breach_notification, para 18 (p.8)].

q28.question: Why does the type of data matter when a company judges how risky a breach is?
q28.answer: The type and sensitivity of personal data are key factors in assessing risk because they directly influence the potential severity of harm to the individuals affected [edpb_breach_notification, para 107 (p.24)]. Generally, more sensitive data—such as health, financial, or identity information—carries a higher risk of damage, such as identity theft, fraud, or discrimination [edpb_breach_notification, paras 102, 108 (pp.23-24)]. Furthermore, the context matters: even seemingly innocuous data can become sensitive depending on what it reveals about an individual, and combinations of different data points often increase the risk compared to a single piece of data [edpb_breach_notification, paras 108-109 (p.24)].

q30.question: Can a service provider choose which software to use for a job without becoming a controller?
q30.answer: A processor may be allowed to choose the technical and organisational means to serve the controller's interests, provided they do not determine the purposes and essential means of the processing [edpb_controller_processor, front matter (p.1)]. While a controller must decide the "why" and "how" of the processing, practical aspects of implementation—referred to as "non-essential means"—can be left to the processor [edpb_controller_processor, front matter (p.1)]. However, if a processor goes beyond the controller's instructions and begins to determine its own purposes and means, it will be considered a controller for that processing [edpb_controller_processor, front matter (p.1)].

q31.question: Does the GDPR set specific duties for a company just because it receives data from another company?
q31.answer: The GDPR's duties for a company receiving data depend on whether it acts as a "processor" or a "controller." If a company processes data on behalf of another entity, it is a processor and must follow documented instructions, ensure confidentiality, implement security measures, and enter into a binding contract [gdpr, Article 28(3); edpb_controller_processor, para 114 (p.34)]. If the receiving company determines the purposes and means of processing independently, it is a separate controller and must fulfill its own obligations under the GDPR, such as providing information to data subjects [edpb_controller_processor, para 70 (p.24), para 5 (p.1)].
